lessons.title: Hello, JVM: compile and run
lessons.body:
## The pipeline

Java source (`.java`) is compiled by `javac` into **bytecode** (`.class`), which the **JVM** runs. Write once, run anywhere — the JVM abstracts the OS/CPU.

## Anatomy

- Every app has an entry point: `public static void main(String[] args)`.
- Class name must match the file name for public classes.

## Modern shortcut

Since Java 11 you can run a single file directly: `java Hello.java` (no explicit compile step). Java 21+ even allows unnamed classes and instance `main` in preview.

lessons.title: Primitives, variables, and var
lessons.body:
## Eight primitives

`byte`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `float`, `double`, `char`, `boolean`. They hold values directly (not references) and have fixed sizes.

## Wrappers

Each primitive has an object wrapper (`Integer`, `Long`, `Boolean`...). Autoboxing converts between them, but beware `NullPointerException` when unboxing a `null` wrapper.

## Local type inference

`var` (Java 10+) infers the type from the initializer for **local variables** only. It is still statically typed — not dynamic.

codeSamples.title: Declarations

lessons.title: Operators and control flow
lessons.body:
## Operators

Arithmetic (`+ - * / %`), comparison (`== != < >`), logical (`&& || !`). `&&` and `||` short-circuit.

## Branching

`if/else`, and the modern **switch expression** (Java 14+) with arrow labels returns a value and requires no `break`.

## Loops

`for`, enhanced `for` (for-each), `while`, `do/while`. Use `break`/`continue` sparingly.

codeSamples.title: Switch expression

lessons.title: Strings, text blocks, and formatting
lessons.body:
## Immutability

`String` is immutable — every modification creates a new object. Use `StringBuilder` for loops that build text.

## Comparison

Use `.equals()` for value equality; `==` compares references. `.equalsIgnoreCase()` for case-insensitive checks.

## Text blocks

Triple-quoted `"""` blocks (Java 15+) preserve multi-line formatting. Use `String.format` or `formatted` for interpolation-like output.

lessons.title: Arrays and the Arrays utility
lessons.body:
## Fixed size

Arrays have a fixed length set at creation (`new int[5]`). Access is zero-based; out-of-range throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

## Helpers

`java.util.Arrays` gives `sort`, `fill`, `copyOf`, `equals`, and `toString` (use it instead of printing an array directly).

## 2D arrays

Java uses arrays-of-arrays, so rows can have different lengths (jagged).

lessons.title: Methods, overloading, and varargs
lessons.body:
## Signatures

A method has a return type, name, and parameter list. `void` returns nothing.

## Overloading

Same name, different parameter types/counts. Resolved at **compile time** by argument types.

## Varargs

`Type... args` accepts zero or more arguments as an array. Only one varargs parameter allowed, and it must be last.

codeSamples.title: Varargs sum

lessons.title: Classes, objects, and constructors
lessons.body:
## Blueprint vs instance

A class defines fields (state) and methods (behavior). `new` creates an instance and runs a constructor.

## Encapsulation

Make fields `private` and expose behavior through methods. This keeps invariants safe.

## this and constructors

`this` refers to the current instance. Constructors can call one another with `this(...)`; a subclass calls the parent with `super(...)`.

codeSamples.title: A small class

lessons.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
lessons.body:
## extends

A subclass inherits fields/methods and can `@Override` behavior. Every class ultimately extends `Object`.

## Polymorphism

A variable of the parent type can hold a subclass instance; the actual method called is chosen at runtime (dynamic dispatch).

## final and abstract

`final` prevents overriding/subclassing. `abstract` classes cannot be instantiated and may declare methods without bodies.

Prefer **composition over inheritance** when the relationship is not a true "is-a".

codeSamples.title: Override and dispatch

lessons.title: Interfaces and default methods
lessons.body:
## Contracts

An interface declares behavior without state. A class `implements` one or many interfaces — Java's answer to multiple inheritance.

## Default and static methods

Interfaces can carry `default` method bodies (added in Java 8) and `static` helpers. Use defaults to evolve APIs without breaking implementers.

## Functional interfaces

An interface with a single abstract method (SAM) can be implemented with a lambda. `@FunctionalInterface` documents that intent.

codeSamples.title: Interface + lambda

lessons.title: Enums, records, and sealed types
lessons.body:
## Enums

Type-safe constants that can carry fields and methods. Great for fixed sets like states or roles.

## Records

`record` (Java 16+) is an immutable data carrier — it generates constructor, accessors, `equals`, `hashCode`, and `toString`. Perfect for DTOs and value objects.

## Sealed types

`sealed` classes/interfaces (Java 17+) restrict which types may extend them, enabling exhaustive `switch` pattern matching.

codeSamples.title: Record + enum

lessons.title: Exceptions and try-with-resources
lessons.body:
## Checked vs unchecked

**Checked** exceptions (`IOException`) must be declared or caught. **Unchecked** (`RuntimeException` subclasses like `NullPointerException`) need not be.

## try/catch/finally

`finally` always runs — for cleanup. Prefer **try-with-resources** for anything `AutoCloseable`; it closes resources automatically, even on exceptions.

## Good hygiene

Catch specific types, never swallow exceptions silently, and add context to messages.

codeSamples.title: try-with-resources

lessons.title: Collections: List, Set, Map
lessons.body:
## The core interfaces

- `List` — ordered, indexed, allows duplicates (`ArrayList`, `LinkedList`).
- `Set` — no duplicates (`HashSet`, `LinkedHashSet`, `TreeSet`).
- `Map` — key/value (`HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap`, `TreeMap`).

## Choosing

`ArrayList` for random access; `ArrayDeque` for stack/queue. `HashMap` for O(1) lookup, `TreeMap` for sorted keys.

## Factory methods

`List.of`, `Set.of`, `Map.of` create **immutable** collections. Copy into a mutable one if you need to modify.

codeSamples.title: Map operations

lessons.title: Generics and bounded wildcards
lessons.body:
## Why generics

Compile-time type safety without casts. `List<String>` guarantees only strings go in and come out.

## Type erasure

Generics are erased at runtime — you cannot do `new T[]` or `instanceof List<String>`. This is why reflection sees raw types.

## PECS

**Producer Extends, Consumer Super**: `? extends T` to read, `? super T` to write. Bounded wildcards make APIs flexible.

codeSamples.title: Bounded method

lessons.title: Lambdas and functional interfaces
lessons.body:
## Lambdas

Concise implementations of SAM interfaces. Capture effectively-final locals.

## Method references

`Class::method`, `instance::method`, and `Class::new` are shorthand for lambdas that just call one method.

## Standard functional types

`Function<T,R>`, `Predicate<T>`, `Consumer<T>`, `Supplier<T>`, `BiFunction` live in `java.util.function` and power the Streams API.

codeSamples.title: Predicate and method ref

lessons.title: The Streams API
lessons.body:
## Pipeline shape

Source -> intermediate ops (`map`, `filter`, `sorted`) -> terminal op (`collect`, `reduce`, `forEach`). Intermediate ops are **lazy**; nothing runs until the terminal op.

## Collectors

`Collectors.toList`, `groupingBy`, `partitioningBy`, `joining` cover most needs. Java 16+ adds `Stream.toList()`.

## Pitfalls

Don't mutate shared state inside a stream. Avoid streams for trivial loops — clarity first. Parallel streams help only for large CPU-bound work.

codeSamples.title: Group by

lessons.title: Optional and null-safety
lessons.body:
## Intent

`Optional<T>` models "maybe a value" for **return types** — signaling absence without `null`.

## Use it well

Chain with `map`, `filter`, `orElse`, `orElseThrow`. Avoid `Optional.get()` without a presence check.

## Anti-patterns

Don't use `Optional` for fields or method parameters, and never return `null` from a method declared to return `Optional`.

codeSamples.title: Chained Optional

lessons.title: equals, hashCode, and immutability
lessons.body:
## The contract

If two objects are `equals`, they **must** have the same `hashCode`. Break this and `HashMap`/`HashSet` behave unpredictably.

## Rules

Override both together, use the same fields in each, and keep those fields immutable if the object is a map key.

## Records help

`record` generates a correct `equals`/`hashCode` for you — a strong reason to use them for value objects.

codeSamples.title: Objects helpers

lessons.title: Files and NIO.2
lessons.body:
## java.nio.file

`Path` and `Files` are the modern API. Read a whole file with `Files.readString`, stream lines with `Files.lines` (close the stream!), write with `Files.writeString`.

## Buffering

For large data use buffered readers/writers or channels. Always use try-with-resources.

## Encoding

Specify `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` explicitly — don't rely on the platform default.

lessons.title: Testing with JUnit 5
lessons.body:
## Structure

`@Test` methods, `@BeforeEach`/`@AfterEach` for setup/teardown. Use AssertJ or JUnit assertions (`assertEquals`, `assertThrows`).

## Parameterized tests

`@ParameterizedTest` with `@ValueSource`/`@CsvSource` runs the same logic over many inputs — the Java equivalent of table-driven tests.

## Mocking

Mockito stubs collaborators. Prefer real objects for value logic; mock only true external boundaries.

lessons.title: Build tools and dependency management
lessons.body:
## Maven vs Gradle

**Maven** uses declarative `pom.xml`; **Gradle** uses a Groovy/Kotlin DSL and incremental builds. Both resolve transitive dependencies from repositories.

## Semantic versioning

Pin versions; use a BOM (bill of materials) to align a family of libraries (e.g. Spring). Watch for version conflicts (`dependency:tree`).

## Modules

The Java Platform Module System (`module-info.java`) enforces strong encapsulation; many apps still run on the classpath.

codeSamples.code:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
  <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
  <version>5.11.0</version>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

lessons.title: HashMap internals and performance
lessons.body:
## Buckets

`HashMap` stores entries in buckets indexed by `hash(key)`. Collisions form a linked list; past a threshold (8 entries) a bucket **treeifies** into a red-black tree for O(log n) lookup.

## Resizing

At load factor 0.75 the table doubles and rehashes — pre-size with `new HashMap<>(expectedSize)` for known large maps to avoid churn.

## Keys

Good, immutable `hashCode`s spread entries evenly. Mutable keys that change after insertion get lost.

codeSamples.title: Pre-sizing
codeSamples.code:
// avoid repeated resizes for a known count
var map = new HashMap<String, Integer>(1024);

lessons.title: Threads, executors, and futures
lessons.body:
## Don't manage raw threads

Use an `ExecutorService` to submit tasks and reuse threads. `Future` represents a pending result; `CompletableFuture` composes async stages.

## Thread safety

Shared mutable state needs coordination: `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, or concurrent collections (`ConcurrentHashMap`).

## Atomics

`AtomicInteger`/`AtomicReference` give lock-free read-modify-write via CAS for simple counters and flags.

lessons.title: JMM, volatile, and happens-before
lessons.body:
## Why this matters

Senior Java interviews dig past `synchronized` into **visibility**, **atomicity**, and the **Java Memory Model (JMM)**. `volatile` guarantees visibility and ordering for a single field — not atomic compound updates.

## Rules of thumb

- Use `volatile` for a **flag** or **publication** of an immutable reference.
- Use `AtomicInteger` / CAS for **read-modify-write**.
- Prefer higher-level tools (`ConcurrentHashMap`, `CompletableFuture`, virtual threads) over hand-rolled locks.

## Happens-before (practical)

If action A *happens-before* B, B sees A's writes. Unlock of a monitor happens-before a subsequent lock of the same monitor. A write to `volatile` happens-before a subsequent read of that same field.

## Double-checked locking

Classic singleton DCL is only correct when the instance field is `volatile`. In practice, prefer a static holder or `ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent`.

codeSamples.title: Volatile shutdown flag

lessons.title: Virtual threads vs CompletableFuture
lessons.body:
## Virtual threads (JEP 444)

Lightweight, JVM-managed threads. Millions can exist because blocking I/O unmounts them from carrier OS threads.

**Use for:** I/O-bound request handling, JDBC, HTTP clients — keep imperative style.

**Watch for:** pinning inside `synchronized` on hot paths (prefer `ReentrantLock` in Java 21; much improved in Java 24+).

## CompletableFuture

Better when you need **explicit composition** of independent async stages, custom executors, or existing reactive APIs.

## Spring Boot tip

Enable with `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`. Prefer MVC + virtual threads over WebFlux unless you need reactive backpressure end-to-end.

codeSamples.title: Virtual thread per task

lessons.title: Spring Boot production pitfalls
lessons.body:
## Constructor injection

Prefer constructor DI — dependencies are explicit, final fields are immutable, tests stay honest.

## `@Transactional` traps

- Self-invocation bypasses the proxy — the annotation does nothing.
- `REQUIRES_NEW` opens a new connection; under load it can exhaust HikariCP.
- Read-only transactions still hold a connection for the method duration.

## HikariCP

Size the pool for **real concurrent DB users**, not "number of threads". With virtual threads, many more requests can wait on the pool — monitor wait time and leaks.

## Collections internals (interview favorites)

Know `HashMap` resize, treeification, and why `ConcurrentHashMap` does not lock the whole map for reads.

codeSamples.title: Constructor injection

lessons.title: Garbage collection and JVM tuning
lessons.body:
## Generational heap

Most objects die young. The GC collects the **young generation** cheaply and promotes survivors to the **old generation**.

## Collectors

**G1** is the default balanced collector. **ZGC** and **Shenandoah** target sub-millisecond pauses for large heaps. Pick based on latency vs throughput goals.

## Practical tuning

Set `-Xms`/`-Xmx` equal in containers, size against the container memory limit, and measure with GC logs (`-Xlog:gc`), JFR, and heap dumps before tweaking flags.

codeSamples.title: Container-aware flags
codeSamples.code:
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms512m -Xmx512m \
  -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log -jar app.jar
